evaluation_policy.decision: Keep or revise the skill based on grounded requirement defects found without inventing product requirements.
evaluation_policy.unique_coverage: Ambiguous specification interpretation, evidence-grounded findings, and scope restraint; activation is a separate population.
evaluation_policy.rerun_when: Specification-review instructions or native discovery changes; replay saved answers for rubric or parser repairs.
evaluation_policy.model_required: Whether a proposed requirement follows from the supplied specification still needs calibrated semantic review.

skill_description: Apply before implementation when writing or reviewing a spec, requirement, acceptance criterion, user story, or ticket. Probe only applicable data-shape edges and bespoke prohibitions, and give every raised item an auditable disposition.

split_policy.tune: The complete public trigger and behavior corpus. Standard local runs exercise every public case.
split_policy.holdout: Unused. Public cases are not represented as secret evidence.
split_policy.holdback: Not committed. A separate operator-held corpus is required before any generalization or promotion claim.

cases.prompt: Before engineering starts, review these acceptance criteria for a bulk import flow and identify the decisions they leave open.
Challenge this user story before we estimate it. I need the edge conditions and product commitments that are still unstated.
We are finalizing a ticket for overdue-payment reminders. What must the ticket decide or rule out before anyone writes code?
We have not selected an implementation. Scrutinize this feature request for boundary cases and outcomes the team would regret committing to by accident.
The deployed invoice worker duplicates a charge after a timeout. Trace the current code, identify the cause, and patch it with a regression check.
Explain how the current retry queue deduplicates requests and point me to the files that own the behavior.
Write a short launch announcement for the new payment reminder feature. Keep the tone reassuring and practical.
The feature is implemented and ready for staging. Exercise the import screen and list the defects you can reproduce.

Review billing-spec.md before implementation. Identify the decisions each source requirement leaves open, distinguish them from facts the draft already settles, and give an arithmetic-consistent coverage summary if you use counts. Use a Markdown table, bullets, or prose. Do not choose unstated product behavior.
expected_behavior: For SP-101, preserves the inclusive 1 through 50 range and asks which whole-percentage rounding rule applies.
For SP-102, keeps empty-list behavior settled while asking about touching windows and equal-start ordering.
For SP-103, keeps blank rejection and the 24-character limit settled while asking what counts as a character.
For SP-104, preserves the at-most-one-ledger-entry backstop while asking which effect wins under concurrent retries.
Uses only source-supported dispositions and reports internally consistent counts if it chooses to count.

graded_dimensions.name: requirement-grounding
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = The answer covers the exact four open decisions: SP-101 rounding rule, SP-102 touching and equal-start behavior, SP-103 character definition, and SP-104 concurrent winner, while preserving every settled range, empty, blank, and backstop fact. 4 = One question is imprecise, but none is generic or invented. 3 = A material source fact or open decision is missing. 2 = Several questions are detached from their requirements. 1 = The response is a taxonomy recital or chooses unstated behavior.

graded_dimensions.name: completeness-and-restraint
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = The review covers every material open edge, preserves settled facts and backstops, and does not choose product behavior. 4 = One minor edge is missing, with no wrong disposition. 3 = A material edge is missing or one settled fact is reopened. 2 = Several gaps or dispositions are wrong. 1 = The response is materially incomplete or writes the missing policy itself.

cases.prompt: Review handoff-spec.md before implementation. Turn its vague quality statement into the concrete product decision the team still needs to make. Use a Markdown table, bullets, or prose. Do not invent numeric, collection, text, stateful, or input-output mechanics when the requirement does not support them.
expected_behavior: Treats HP-201's words calm and useful as an unresolved observable product-quality decision.
Does not invent numeric, collection, text, stateful, or input-output mechanics.

graded_dimensions.name: requirement-grounding
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = The single question turns the supplied phrase into a concrete product decision without inventing a data shape. 4 = The question is grounded but slightly broad. 3 = It is a generic quality question. 2 = It invents mechanics absent from the requirement. 1 = It ignores or copies the requirement.

graded_dimensions.name: restraint
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = The response keeps the prose requirement unclassified and asks only for an observable product decision. 4 = The classification is restrained but one phrase is vague. 3 = It adds one weakly supported mechanism. 2 = It invents several data-shape mechanics. 1 = It replaces the requirement with an unrelated taxonomy.

cases.prompt: Review reminder-spec.md before implementation. Separate ordinary edge questions from concrete limits on what this reminder may become. Tie each item to its source requirement, preserve the trained-reviewer backstop, and refer generic security or compliance topics to their owners instead of expanding them here. Use a Markdown table, bullets, or prose.
expected_behavior: For RR-301, preserves the two-reminders-per-calendar-day limit and asks which timezone defines the day.
For RR-302, preserves SMS or email, first-name and overdue-amount use, and the trained-reviewer backstop.
Raises two or three concrete dignity, audience-exposure, consent, data-use, or fairness limits instead of a generic safety catalogue.
Keeps generic security and compliance ownership outside this focused review.

graded_dimensions.name: bespoke-product-restraint
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = Each prohibition states a concrete unwanted reminder outcome tied to the supplied channel, debt details, or repayment goal, and it is framed as a decision or criterion. 4 = The items are specific, with one minor abstraction. 3 = The list mixes bespoke concerns with generic privacy, fairness, or security slogans. 2 = Most items could be pasted into any product. 1 = No bespoke prohibition is present, or the response invents a legal mandate.

graded_dimensions.name: edge-coverage-and-state
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = RR-301's timezone gap is explicit; RR-302 preserves the channel, allowed data, repayment goal, and trained-reviewer backstop while surfacing concrete audience, consent, data-use, or fairness limits without deciding them. 4 = One minor edge is missing. 3 = A material edge or settled fact is missing. 2 = Several items are detached from their source. 1 = The response selects policy, removes the backstop, or substitutes a generic safety catalogue.

cases.prompt: Review choice-spec.md before implementation. Surface the unresolved product choices under each source requirement without selecting an answer. Keep explicit empty-input behavior settled. Use a Markdown table, bullets, or prose.
expected_behavior: Keeps CH-401 touching-window behavior and CH-402 character definition unresolved.
Preserves CH-401 empty-list behavior and CH-402 null and blank rejection as settled.
Allows different grounded wording for the same unresolved choices.

graded_dimensions.name: requirement-grounding
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = Each question states the exact unresolved choice and does not choose for the product owner. 4 = Both choices are grounded, with one imprecise phrase. 3 = Questions are relevant but generic. 2 = A choice is invented or silently selected. 1 = The response parrots categories without reviewing the supplied requirements.

graded_dimensions.name: settled-fact-restraint
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = The review covers all material open choices while preserving both explicit empty-input rules. 4 = One minor detail is vague. 3 = One open choice is missed or one settled rule is reopened. 2 = Several states are wrong. 1 = The response chooses an answer or contradicts the supplied behavior.

cases.prompt: Review settings-spec.md before implementation. List the acceptance tests you would write for each requirement and the decisions it still leaves open. Use a Markdown table, bullets, or prose. Do not choose unstated product behavior.
expected_behavior: For SL-501, preserves the inclusive 1 through 300 range and the rejection of values outside it as settled.

For SL-501, checks the empty-value edge in each of YAML, TOML, and JSON, such as a bare YAML key or `~`, TOML having no null at all, and JSON `null` or an empty string, instead of once for the settings file.
For SL-501, checks the integer edge per format, such as `300.0`, a quoted `"30"`, or a format-specific integer spelling, or states why checking one format covers the others.

For SL-502, treats the example's read order as illustration and proposes a test that reads the user file first and still expects the user value, as the override rule states. The example's use of TOML for both files may become an open question or a test under a stated assumption.
Leaves unstated behavior open, such as whether an empty user value falls back to the default or keeps the project value.

graded_dimensions.name: variant-coverage
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = SL-501's empty-value and integer edges are each checked in YAML, TOML, and JSON, with at least one format-specific difference named, such as TOML having no null, or the response gives a sound reason why checking one format covers the others. 4 = Every format is checked for one of the two edges, and the other edge is raised once with no wrong claim about any format. 3 = The edges are raised once for the settings file, with no per-format check. 2 = Formats are named, but no edge is tied to a format. 1 = No SL-501 edge is raised, a format behavior is misstated, or the response chooses unstated behavior.

graded_dimensions.name: example-restraint
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = SL-502's read order is treated as a property of the example, not a rule, and a proposed test reads the user file first and still expects the user value. The single format may be tested under a stated assumption or left open. 4 = The read-order test is present but conditional or vaguely worded. 3 = No proposed test breaks an incidental property of the example, and the tests only replay or generalize it. 2 = The response makes read order or the example's format a rule. 1 = SL-502 is ignored, its override rule is contradicted, or the response chooses unstated behavior.

cases.prompt: We're about to build the job config loader that sync-job-spec.md describes. Write out its acceptance criteria before implementation starts. A Markdown table, bullets, or prose is fine.
expected_behavior: Keeps SJ-101's missing-field rejection, SJ-102's relative-path rejection, and SJ-104's 1 through 90 range and its rejection as settled.

Adds no criterion that expects a rejection, error, or rewrite that no requirement states, such as one on a `destination` form, an unknown key, or a duplicate key. The `backup://` scheme appears only in SJ-103's example, and SJ-102's absolute-path rule names only `source`.
Leaves the supported `destination` forms open, or states that no requirement restricts them. A criterion that the example value loads is fine.

graded_dimensions.name: unrequested-rejection
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = Every rejection, error, or rewrite that a proposed test or criterion expects traces to a stated rule: SJ-101's missing fields, SJ-102's requirement that `source` be an absolute path, or SJ-104's integer range. Inputs that no requirement restricts stay open questions or are stated as unrestricted. Examples are a `destination` without the `backup://` scheme, a relative `destination`, an empty or null `destination`, an unknown key, and a duplicate key. Rejecting a `source` value because it is not an absolute path counts as traced to SJ-102. Rejecting a file that is empty, does not parse as YAML, or has no mapping at the top level counts as traced to SJ-101, because it has neither field. An open policy question explicitly excluded from tests or criteria is unresolved, even if it recommends an answer; it is not an expected rejection. 4 = Every expected rejection traces to a stated rule, but the open question about `destination` forms is missing or vague. 3 = One or two untraced rejections appear as criteria, including ones marked as proposals for the spec owner to confirm. 2 = Three or more untraced rejections appear as criteria. 1 = A stated rejection is reversed, or a criterion rejects a `destination` form, such as one taken from SJ-102's rule or the `backup://` example.

graded_dimensions.name: stated-rejections-kept
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = SJ-101's missing-field rejection, SJ-102's relative-path rejection, and SJ-104's range rejection are all covered, with `keep` checked at 0, 1, 90, and 91 or an equivalent boundary set. 4 = All three rejections are covered, with one `keep` boundary missing. 3 = One stated rejection is missing. 2 = Several stated rejections are missing. 1 = A stated rejection is contradicted or left open as undecided.

cases.prompt: Before we add the archive settings in sync-job-archive.md to the loader in sync_job_loader.py, write the acceptance criteria for them. sync-job-spec.md is the original spec, and nightly.yaml is one of the job configs that runs today. A Markdown table, bullets, or prose is fine.
expected_behavior: Keeps nightly.yaml loading as it does today, including its `destination`, which is a plain path rather than a `backup://` URL.

Adds no rejection that no requirement states: none on the form of `archive_destination` or `destination`, such as an absolute-path rule copied from `source` or a `backup://` rule taken from the examples, none on an `archive_destination` equal to `destination`, none on `archive_after_days` set without `archive_destination`, and none on an unknown key. These stay open or unrestricted.
Covers SJ-202's 1 through 365 range at its boundaries and the rejection of `archive_destination` without `archive_after_days`.

graded_dimensions.name: unrequested-rejection
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = Every rejection, error, or rewrite that a proposed test or criterion expects traces to a stated rule: SJ-202's integer range, SJ-202's rejection of `archive_destination` without `archive_after_days`, or a rule the current loader already enforces. Inputs that no requirement restricts stay open questions or are stated as unrestricted. Examples are an `archive_destination` or `destination` form, such as an absolute-path rule copied from `source` or a `backup://` rule taken from the examples, an `archive_destination` equal to `destination`, `archive_after_days` set without `archive_destination`, and an unknown key. An open policy question explicitly excluded from tests or criteria is unresolved, even if it recommends an answer; it is not an expected rejection. 4 = Every expected rejection traces to a stated rule, but the open choices are missing or vague. 3 = One or two untraced rejections appear as criteria, including ones marked as proposals for the spec owner to confirm. 2 = Three or more untraced rejections appear as criteria. 1 = A proposed rule would reject nightly.yaml, or a stated rejection is reversed.

graded_dimensions.name: accepted-input-kept
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = A test or criterion loads nightly.yaml, or an equivalent config with a plain-path `destination` and no archive fields, and expects the same result as today. SJ-202's range is covered at 0, 1, 365, and 366 or an equivalent boundary set, and so is the rejection of `archive_destination` without `archive_after_days`. 4 = nightly.yaml is kept working and both SJ-202 rejections are covered, but one SJ-202 boundary is missing. 3 = Neither nightly.yaml nor an equivalent config is covered, though nothing proposed would break it. 2 = A proposed rule would break nightly.yaml under some reading. 1 = A proposed rule rejects nightly.yaml, or a stated SJ-202 rejection is dropped.

cases.prompt: Another team owns signup-spec.md and we can't change it. We're about to build the signup handler it describes. Write the acceptance tests it should pass before implementation starts. A test name plus a line on its input and expected result is enough for each.
expected_behavior: Separates SU-302's trimming from SU-304's stripping with whitespace inside a value: an `invite_code` with inner whitespace that matches an open invite once all whitespace is removed returns 201, and a `display_name` with inner whitespace is saved with it.
Ties each test to a quoted spec sentence that gives its expected result, and writes no test whose result no requirement gives. Such an answer is listed apart as an assumption or open question.

graded_dimensions.name: contrast-test
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = The tests put whitespace inside a value and check both rules: an `invite_code` with inner whitespace that matches an open invite once all whitespace is removed still finds it under SU-304, and a `display_name` or `email` with inner whitespace keeps it under SU-302. One test or two together cover both, so they fail if trimming and stripping are implemented as the same operation either way. 4 = The `invite_code` inner-whitespace test is present and expects the invite to be found, but no test checks that trimming keeps inner whitespace. 3 = Inner whitespace is tested only for `display_name` or `email`, or the inner-whitespace invite code is raised only as an open question though SU-304 settles it, or whitespace is tested only at the start and end of values. 2 = The tests treat trimming and stripping as one operation, for example by expecting the same result from both on a value with inner whitespace, or expect an `invite_code` with inner whitespace to return 403 although it matches an open invite once stripped. 1 = No test touches trimming or stripping, or a test contradicts SU-302 or SU-304.

graded_dimensions.name: spec-citations
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = Every proposed test is tied, and the response proposes no test whose result no requirement gives. A test is tied when it quotes the spec sentence or example that gives its expected result, or names one the response quotes elsewhere. An open question kept out of the tests is not a test. 4 = No test expects a result that no requirement gives, but exactly one test is not tied and more than half are. 3 = More than half of the tests are tied but two or more are not, or one test expects a result that no requirement gives. A test labeled as an assumption counts. 2 = Half or fewer of the tests are tied, or two or more tests expect results that no requirement gives. 1 = No test quotes or names any spec text. When two levels fit, give the lower.

cases.prompt: We're about to build the import command that pantry-spec.md describes. Write the acceptance tests it should pass before implementation starts. A test name plus a line on its input and expected result is enough for each.
expected_behavior: Numbers a skipped crate by its line in the delivery sheet, header counted, so the first crate is `line 2`, as PN-603's "line number in the delivery sheet" says.
Gives a crate with both faults one report line that holds both reasons, and counts it once in `skipped`, as PN-603's "For each skipped crate the report has one line" says.
Counts crates, not `units`, in `shelved`, as PN-604 says, with a shelved crate whose `units` is above 1.
Treats the example, which has one crate of one unit and no skipped crate, as passing under every reading, so it settles none of the three.

graded_dimensions.name: unit-settled-by-spec-noun
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = No test is wrong and all three units are settled. The units: (a) A skipped crate is reported with its line number in the sheet, header counted, so the first crate is `line 2`. (b) One crate with both faults gives one report line that holds both reasons and adds 1 to `skipped`. (c) A shelved crate whose `units` is above 1 adds 1 to `shelved`. A unit is settled when a test's input makes the plausible units differ and the test states the result the spec's wording gives, as in (a) to (c). One test can settle more than one unit. A test that states no line number or count, a test whose stated result would be the same under both readings, and a unit left as an open question settle nothing and are not wrong. A test is wrong when it expects the other unit: `line 1` for the first crate, two report lines or `skipped: 2` for one crate with two faults, or a `shelved` figure that sums `units`. 4 = No test is wrong and exactly two units are settled. 3 = No test is wrong and exactly one unit is settled. 2 = No test is wrong and no unit is settled. An answer with no test is here. 1 = At least one test is wrong.

cases.prompt: We're about to build the trails command that trail-spec.md describes. Write the acceptance tests it should pass before implementation starts. A test name plus a line on its input and expected result is enough for each.
expected_behavior: Turns both examples into tests whose expected output is the example's lines verbatim, compared as whole text.

Expects `km` in every output line, the spelling every example shows, though TR-702 also allows `kilometres`. No test of an example accepts either spelling or compares through a parser, pattern, or normalizer. A loose check on a line no example shows still passes the gate.

Expects no rejection for an input because it differs from the example inputs, such as metres that are not whole, zero, or negative, a one-word name, a name that holds a colon, or a name added twice. These are accepted where the spec gives a result, or left open.

graded_dimensions.name: example-output-exact
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = No test expects a wrong form, both examples are exact, and no line outside the examples is checked loosely. The answer may note that TR-702 also allows `kilometres`. It still expects `km`. Give each example one state, from every test that checks its lines. A test checks an example's lines when it runs exactly that example's commands and checks the output, or when it states one check for every `trails list` line. The example is loosened when any such test checks through a parsed number, a regular expression, either spelling accepted, ignored whitespace, or "contains". Otherwise it is exact when such a test's expected output is the example's lines verbatim, compared as whole text. Otherwise it is paraphrased when such tests only describe its output in words. Otherwise it is untested. So a test in words beside a verbatim test of the same example, such as "`--min 5000` does not list Mill path", leaves that example exact. A wrong form is an expected output of `kilometres` or of another form no example shows. The examples' form is name, colon, one space, one decimal place, a space, `km`. Accepting either spelling is a loose check, not a wrong form. A line outside the examples is any other expected output line. TR-702 allows both spellings there, and an example fixes its own lines. Such a line is checked loosely when a test checks it through one of those five ways, or describes it in words, such as "ends with a unit", without writing it out. 4 = No test expects a wrong form, both examples are exact, and at least one line outside the examples is checked loosely. 3 = No test expects a wrong form, each example is exact or loosened, and at least one is loosened. 2 = No test expects a wrong form, at least one example is paraphrased or untested, and the two are not both untested. 1 = A test expects a wrong form, or both examples are untested.

graded_dimensions.name: example-inputs-unrestricted
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = No test is counted, no test contradicts an example, and no test is unbacked. A test is counted when it expects a rejection, an error, or a reinterpretation for an input because it differs from the example inputs. A reinterpretation gives the input a meaning other than the one typed, such as expecting one line after a name is added twice. Inputs that differ include metres that are not whole, zero, or negative, a one-word name, a name that holds a colon, and a name added twice. These are examples of such inputs, not the whole list. A rejection of a `<metres>` that is not a number is not counted either way. A test is unbacked when it is not counted and it expects, for an input that differs from the example inputs, an accepted result that TR-701 to TR-703 do not give. An input that is absent, expected accepted with the result TR-701 to TR-703 give, or listed as open with no test makes no test counted or unbacked. 4 = No test is counted and no test contradicts an example, but at least one test is unbacked. 3 = Exactly one test is counted, it is labeled as an assumption or a proposal, and no test contradicts an example. 2 = Exactly one test is counted, it has no label, and no test contradicts an example. 1 = Two or more tests are counted, or a test contradicts an example.

cases.prompt: Another team owns locker-spec.md and we can't change it. We're implementing the pickup endpoint it describes. Write the acceptance tests the implementation must pass. A test name plus a line on its input and expected result is enough for each.
expected_behavior: Ties every test to a quoted spec sentence or example line that gives its expected result.

Writes no test for an answer the spec does not give: the response for a `locker` that names no locker, whether a 422 counts toward or breaks LK-403's run of three wrong pins, and the exact 72-hour instant. Lists these apart as assumptions or open gaps, and says the implementation takes the permissive behavior. A test may expect 422 for a `pin` sent as a JSON number, from LK-402, or 403 for the pin of a returned parcel, from LK-404 with LK-403.
Pairs LK-402's rejection with accepted pins at both bounds and with a leading-zero pin such as the example's `0417`, and pairs LK-403's lockout with a right pin after two wrong ones.

graded_dimensions.name: only-stated-results-tested
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = Every test's expected result is given by a spec sentence or the example. Whether a test quotes its source is graded by another assertion, not here. Each answer the spec does not give is kept out of the tests and listed apart as an assumption or open gap, with at least two of these three: a `locker` that names no locker, whether a 422 counts toward or breaks LK-403's run of three wrong pins, the exact 72-hour instant. For at least one, the answer says the implementation takes the permissive or least restrictive behavior and that no test asserts it. The spec gives two results that look open, so a test for either is not counted against the answer, and neither is leaving it out: 422 for a `pin` that is not a string of four to six digits, such as a JSON number (LK-402's "Any other `pin` returns 422"), and 403 for a pin where no parcel waits, such as after LK-404's return (LK-404's "its pin stops working" with LK-403). 4 = No test asserts an answer the spec does not give, but the answer lists apart fewer than two of the three named above, or for none of them does it say both that the implementation takes the permissive or least restrictive behavior and that no test asserts it. 3 = One or two tests assert an answer the spec does not give. A test labeled as an assumption, a proposal, or "to confirm" counts. 2 = Three or more tests assert such answers. 1 = A test contradicts a stated rule, or most tests decide unstated answers with no label. When two levels fit, give the lower.

graded_dimensions.name: quoted-sources
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = Every counted test is tied. A test is tied when it quotes the spec sentence or example line that gives its expected result, or names that sentence or line, by ID or as the example, where the answer quotes it elsewhere. A requirement ID whose sentence the answer never quotes ties nothing. Count only proposed tests whose result the spec gives: a test for an answer the spec does not give is graded by another assertion, and an open question kept out of the tests is not a test. 4 = Exactly one counted test is not tied, and more than half are tied. 3 = Two or more counted tests are not tied, and more than half are tied. 2 = At least one counted test is tied, and half or fewer are. 1 = No counted test is tied, or the answer has no counted test.

graded_dimensions.name: rejections-paired
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = LK-402's rejection is tested, no test rejects a valid pin, both bounds are rejected, and the tests give all four accepted neighbors. Both bounds are rejected when a test expects 422 for a three-digit pin and a test expects 422 for a seven-digit pin. The neighbors: (i) a four-digit pin is not rejected, (ii) a six-digit pin is not rejected, (iii) a pin with a leading zero, such as the example's `0417`, is expected accepted as written, (iv) after two wrong pins the right pin still returns 200. One test can give more than one, so the example alone gives (i) and (iii). 4 = LK-402's rejection is tested, no test rejects a valid pin, both bounds are rejected, and the tests give exactly three of the four. 3 = LK-402's rejection is tested, no test rejects a valid pin, and either the tests give one or two of the four, or they give three or four and at least one of those two 422 tests is missing. 2 = LK-402's rejection is tested, no test rejects a valid pin, and the tests give none of the four. 1 = A test rejects a valid pin, such as one with a leading zero, or LK-402's rejection is not tested.

cases.prompt: Read incident-brief.md. This is a deployed incident, not a pre-build requirements review. Explain the correct next owner and keep the response scoped to the shipped failure. Do not rewrite committed product behavior or manufacture requirements.
expected_behavior: Treats the second charge after a client retry as a deployed incident requiring containment, reproduction, and cause evidence.
Routes the shipped failure to debugging or incident response without manufacturing requirements, coverage counts, or new product behavior.

graded_dimensions.name: scope-and-routing
graded_dimensions.rubric: 5 = The response treats the duplicate charge as a shipped incident, routes it to debugging or incident response, and does not create new requirements. 4 = The route is correct with one vague phrase. 3 = The route is plausible but mixed with requirements advice. 2 = The response materially expands the task. 1 = It rewrites committed product behavior or ignores the incident.
